8. Enterprise checklist, mapped to the code

# Practice Where it shows up here Why it matters
1 Single Responsibility Controller owns one junction's safety; TrafficManagementCenter owns the city view; GreenWaveDesigner owns offset maths; ApproachQueues owns the road surface A routing change never touches signal timing code
2 Open/Closed A new plan is a new TimingStrategy subclass; a new consumer of telemetry is a new TelemetryListener Transit priority or a SPaT broadcaster arrives without editing the controller
3 Liskov Any TimingStrategy is safe in any controller, because the controller clamps greens and owns clearance A plan can be wrong without being dangerous
4 Dependency inversion Controller takes Clock, ApproachQueues, TelemetrySink, config; centre takes CommsNetwork; build_city wires them Tests swap in a recorder or a severed link with no mocks
5 Typed errors errors.py: 10 subclasses of TrafficError; the one except Exception, in EventBus.send, logs and is commented The centre retries a conflict and a lost link differently
6 logging, not print Mode changes at WARNING (INFO for recovery), missed preemptions at ERROR; print only in __main__.py An operator can route the ERRORs to a pager
7 Validate at boundaries Config __post_init__, GreenSplit, CoordinatedPlan fit check, TimeOfDayPlan ordering, lane counts, negative arrivals, heartbeat interval at register() A bad plan is rejected before it reaches a signal
8 Config via dataclass SafetyTimings, AdaptiveTuning, DischargeConfig, FailsafeConfig, ControllerConfig, TmcConfig Every timing in the city is auditable in one file
9 Composition over inheritance TimeOfDayPlan holds other plans; the controller holds a plan, a sink and queues; the city is assembled in build_city Behaviour changes by plugging in, not by subclassing the controller
10 Thread-safety RLock per controller; locks in clock, queues, bus, uplink, network, centre; documented lock order; leaf _status_lock Commands, sensors and the sim loop can share a controller safely; pinned by the concurrency test
11 Repository pattern Not needed in this slice: the centre's desired-plan map is the obvious seam for a PlanRepository when plans must survive a centre restart Honest about scope; the seam is named
12 unittest incl. edge cases 51 tests: heartbeat exactly at the limit, plans below the minimum, off-beat cycles, dropped telemetry, conflicting preemption, forgotten releases The failure paths are the product here

Honest limits. The comms model is binary: up or down. Real links lose some packets and delay others. The queue model is one lane-group per axis with a constant saturation flow. Coordination only runs on the NS axis of a corridor, and two crossing corridors would need a shared cycle length. Locks cover threads in one process; a real centre is several processes, and the desired-plan map would live in a database.

9. Common interview follow-ups

"Now add transit signal priority for buses." Priority is a softer cousin of preemption. A late bus may get a few extra seconds of green or an early green, but it never cuts a cross street short. The design change is a new request type, say PriorityRequest(axis, max_extension), and a controller method that adjusts _duration of the current or next green within a cap from config. Preemption still outranks it. The transition table does not change at all, because priority changes durations, not phases.

"Now an incident happens in the middle of an ambulance run." Today a run's legs are fixed at dispatch. The change is a reroute step in report_incident(). Find each active run whose remaining legs use the closed link. Recompute its route from the next pending intersection, release any held legs that are no longer on it, and splice in the new legs with fresh ETAs. The controller needs nothing new. That is the point of keeping routing in the centre and safety in the controller.

"Now scale to 10,000 intersections and three centre nodes." Partition intersections by region, one partition per node, with a message broker carrying heartbeats and telemetry. The desired-plan map moves into a database, and each plan gets a version number so apply_plan() becomes idempotent (ignore a version you already have). Controllers don't change. They already tolerate a silent centre, which is exactly what a node failover looks like from the roadside.

"Now broadcast signal timing to connected cars (SPaT)." Write a new TelemetryListener that turns PhaseChanged and CycleStarted events into "time to next change" messages. The controller, the centre and the bus are untouched. This is the Observer seam paying for itself.

"What if the centre is compromised and pushes a plan with one-second greens?" The controller clamps it to min_green and logs a warning; yellow and all-red were never the plan's to set. That bounds the damage to "slow". In a production design you would add signed plans and a local safety envelope per intersection (maximum cycle length, minimum pedestrian time), checked before apply_plan() stores anything.

"Two ambulances approach one junction on crossing streets." The first preemption wins and the second gets PreemptionConflictError, so the centre keeps its leg pending and retries every second. Once the first vehicle's hold is released, the second is served. A better policy orders conflicting requests by ETA and lets the earlier arrival go first even if it called second. That would be a new PreemptionPolicy strategy inside the controller.

"Why does a controller boot into ALL_RED and local fallback?" Because at power-up it knows nothing. All-red is the only phase that is safe without knowing who was moving a second ago. Local fallback is the only plan it can trust without the centre. It earns CENTRAL by hearing a heartbeat.

"Why not let the adaptive plan end a green early when the queue empties?" You could, and real "gap-out" logic does. It changes the controller, though, not the plan: the decision happens mid-phase, and plans in this design only speak at the cycle boundary. That is a deliberate trade. Plans stay simple and testable, and the cost is some wasted green on quiet approaches.

10. Stretch tasks

  1. Mid-run rerouting. Implement the incident-during-a-run follow-up. Add a test where B-C closes after dispatch and before the ambulance reaches B. Assert that B is released and the run continues through D.
  2. Detector faults. Let ApproachQueues.count() return None when a loop detector fails. Make AdaptivePlan "fail to max" for that axis (use max_green), which is what real controllers do. Decide whether the fault should also be a telemetry event, and defend the choice.
  3. Pedestrian phases. Add NS_WALK and EW_WALK with a ped_clearance timing in SafetyTimings. Update TRANSITIONS and prove with a test that no plan can undercut the pedestrian clearance.
  4. Transit priority. Implement PriorityRequest from the follow-ups, capped by a new config field. Show that a priority request during a preemption is ignored, and one during the cross street's green waits for the cycle.

Chapter 8: Rate Limiter

Type every file in order. Run each checkpoint before moving on. All commands run from the project folder (the one holding rate_limiter/ and tests/). Python 3.13, stdlib only.

The first seven chapters modelled businesses: lots, lifts, libraries, cars. This one models a piece of infrastructure, and it is one of the most-asked LLD problems of 2026. Every public API has a rate limiter in front of it. Every LLM gateway meters tokens per key. Every agent framework hammers some endpoint until a 429 tells it to stop. The problem looks small, a counter and an if. It isn't. Five algorithms compete for the job, the counter is shared by every thread in the process, and the interviewer will eventually ask you to run it on twenty servers at once.

1. The problem

An API serves anonymous visitors, signed-in users, and partners calling with API keys. Each kind of caller gets a limit: so many requests per window of time. Paying tiers get more. When a caller goes over, the API answers 429 Too Many Requests and tells them when to come back. The limiter must be fast, correct under concurrent requests, cheap in memory when a million different IPs pass through, and swappable between algorithms without touching the code that calls it.

You build the limiter itself, not the web server. Its job is to answer one question per request — "may this pass?" — and to answer it with enough detail that the HTTP layer can write the response headers.

2. Requirements

Clarifying questions to ask first (with the answers an interviewer would give):

  • What do we limit on: user, API key, IP? All three. A request is limited by one key, chosen by the caller: user id when signed in, API key for machine clients, IP for anonymous traffic.
  • Same limit for everyone? No. Tiers: anonymous, free, pro, partner. Each scope has a default tier; an explicit tier overrides it.
  • Which algorithm? "Which would you pick, and why?" This is the real question. Expect to compare at least token bucket, fixed window and sliding window, and to name the trade-off of each.
  • Are bursts acceptable? For paid tiers, yes: 1,000 per minute on average, up to 2,000 at once.
  • Does every request cost the same? Not in 2026. An LLM endpoint costs by tokens, a bulk export by rows. Support a per-request cost.
  • What do we send back on a denial? HTTP 429 with Retry-After, plus RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset on every response.
  • One process or many? Start with one. Then expect "now there are twenty API servers".
  • What if the counter store is down? Ask whether the business prefers to fail open (let traffic through) or fail closed (refuse it). Make it a config flag.
  • How many distinct keys? Potentially millions of IPs, most seen once. Idle keys must not live forever.

Functional

  • Decide a request for a ClientKey(scope, value, tier) with a cost (default 1). Return a Decision: allowed, remaining, retry_after, reset_after.
  • Five algorithms behind one interface: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding-window log, sliding-window counter. The rule picks the algorithm.
  • Tiers come from config: name, limit, window, algorithm, optional burst.
  • Map a decision to an HTTP status (200 or 429) and response headers.
  • Purge idle keys, on demand and from a background thread.
  • On a store failure: fail open or fail closed, as configured.

Non-functional

  • Thread-safe: forty threads racing on one key with a limit of 10 let exactly 10 through, for every algorithm.
  • Time is injectable. No algorithm reads the system clock; tests never sleep.
  • State lives behind a storage interface, so a Redis-backed store can replace the dict.
  • O(1) memory per key, except the sliding log, which is O(limit) by design.
  • Typed exceptions; a denial is a normal result, not an exception.
  • Stdlib only.

3. From nouns to classes

Noun in the problem Class Responsibility
A limit, a tier LimitRule One rule: limit, window, algorithm, burst
The tier table RateLimiterConfig Tiers, scope defaults, cleanup and failure knobs
The caller ClientKey Scope + value + optional tier; builds its storage key
Tier lookup RuleBook Turns a ClientKey into a LimitRule
The algorithm RateLimitAlgorithm (+5) Pure step: old state → new state + decision
The verdict Decision allowed / remaining / retry_after, as HTTP
Where counters live StateStore, InMemoryStore Atomic read-modify-write with per-key expiry
Time Clock, MonotonicClock, ManualClock The only source of "now"
The limiter RateLimiter Resolve rule, run algorithm in the store, handle failure
Cleanup IdleKeySweeper Background thread that purges idle keys

4. Class diagram

5. Key design decisions

  1. An algorithm is a pure step function. apply(state, rule, now, cost) returns the next state and a Decision. It reads no clock, takes no lock, does no I/O. That one constraint pays three times. Tests call it directly with made-up timestamps. Thread safety becomes the store's job alone. And the same step can later run inside Redis, because it has nothing in it that only works in Python's memory.
  2. The store owns atomicity. StateStore.update(key, now, ttl, step) reads the state, runs the step, writes the result and sets an expiry, as one atomic unit. "Check, then act" is the classic race in a rate limiter: two threads both read 9 of 10, both write 10, and 11 requests pass. Putting the whole read-modify-write behind one method means no caller can split it by accident. In memory that unit is a lock. In Redis it is a Lua script.
  3. A denial is a value, not an exception. A 429 is the limiter working, not failing. Decision(allowed=False, retry_after=…) flows through the same code path as an allow. Exceptions are kept for things that really are wrong: a broken config, a blank key, a dead store.
  4. One Decision for all five algorithms. The HTTP layer calls decision.headers() and never learns which algorithm ran. Swapping fixed window for token bucket on the free tier is a config change, not a code change.
  5. Each algorithm knows its own memory horizon. idle_ttl(rule) says when a key's state becomes identical to a brand-new key's. A token bucket is full again after capacity / rate seconds. A sliding counter needs two whole windows. The store expires each key at exactly that point, plus a grace period. That makes cleanup safe by construction: deleting an idle key can never hand a client a quota it hadn't earned back.
  6. The rule is part of the storage key. rl:{rule}:{algorithm}:{scope}:{value}. A user who upgrades from free to pro starts a fresh pro bucket instead of inheriting a half-empty free one. Two algorithms never read each other's state shapes.
  7. Monotonic time, injected. Wall-clock time jumps: NTP corrections, a VM resuming. A token bucket fed a clock that jumps forward refills for free. The production clock is time.monotonic(), and every algorithm clamps a negative elapsed time to zero anyway.

The five algorithms, side by side. This is the table the interviewer is fishing for. Learn the "why" column, not just the names.

Algorithm State per key Bursts Accuracy Choose it when
Token bucket 2 floats Up to burst, then average rate Exact for its model You want an average rate with controlled bursts. The default for most APIs.
Leaky bucket 2 floats Queued and smoothed, never passed through at once Exact for its model The downstream needs a steady rate (a payment processor, an SMS gateway). It shapes traffic instead of policing it.
Fixed window window index + count Up to 2× the limit across a boundary Coarse Daily or monthly quotas that line up with billing, where the boundary burst doesn't matter.
Sliding-window log one timestamp per request None Exact Limits are small (say 10 per minute) and exactness matters, like login attempts.
Sliding-window counter window index + 2 counts Negligible Near-exact (assumes even spread in the previous window) Large limits where you want sliding behaviour at O(1) memory.

Patterns, and why each earns its place. Strategy for the algorithms: five ways to answer the same question, chosen per rule. Repository, in the form of StateStore, for state: the dict becomes Redis and the limiter never notices. A registry (dict[str, RateLimitAlgorithm]) instead of an if algorithm == … chain, so a sixth algorithm is a new class plus one dictionary entry.

6. Type along

Step 1 — The error hierarchy

Goal: name every way the limiter can fail. Notice what is missing: there is no RateLimitExceededError.

Type rate_limiter/errors.py:

"""The rate limiter's failure modes, one type per recovery path.

A denied request is NOT an error: it is a normal Decision with allowed=False.
Exceptions are reserved for bad configuration, bad input, and a broken store.
"""


class RateLimiterError(Exception):
    """Root of every rate-limiter failure. Catch this to catch them all."""


class ConfigError(RateLimiterError):
    """The limiter was wired with configuration that can never work."""


class InvalidRuleError(ConfigError):
    """A LimitRule has a non-positive limit, window, or a misplaced burst."""


class UnknownAlgorithmError(ConfigError):
    """A rule names an algorithm nobody registered."""


class InvalidRequestError(RateLimiterError):
    """The caller passed input the limiter refuses to evaluate."""


class InvalidKeyError(InvalidRequestError):
    """The client key is blank."""


class InvalidCostError(InvalidRequestError):
    """The request cost is below 1 or larger than the bucket could ever hold."""


class UnknownTierError(InvalidRequestError):
    """The client asked for a tier, or has a scope, with no configured rule."""


class StoreError(RateLimiterError):
    """The state store failed (in a distributed setup: Redis timed out)."""


class LimiterUnavailableError(RateLimiterError):
    """The store failed and the limiter is configured to fail closed."""

What to notice. Two families with two different owners. ConfigError is the operator's fault and should stop the process at startup. InvalidRequestError is the caller's fault and maps to a 400. StoreError is the infrastructure's fault, and the limiter decides what to do about it from config. A caller that catches InvalidRequestError will never accidentally swallow a dead Redis.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "from rate_limiter.errors import InvalidCostError, InvalidRequestError, RateLimiterError; print(issubclass(InvalidCostError, InvalidRequestError), issubclass(InvalidCostError, RateLimiterError))"

Output:

True True

Step 2 — Configuration: rules, tiers and scopes

Goal: put every number the limiter enforces in one validated place.

Type rate_limiter/config.py:

"""Configuration: algorithms, key scopes, limit rules, and the tier table.

Every number the limiter enforces lives here. The algorithms read a LimitRule;
they never contain a literal limit or window of their own.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import StrEnum

from .errors import ConfigError, InvalidRuleError


class Algorithm(StrEnum):
    """Names of the built-in algorithms. A custom one can use any other string."""

    TOKEN_BUCKET = "token_bucket"
    LEAKY_BUCKET = "leaky_bucket"
    FIXED_WINDOW = "fixed_window"
    SLIDING_LOG = "sliding_log"
    SLIDING_COUNTER = "sliding_counter"


# Only bucket algorithms have a capacity separate from their refill rate.
BUCKET_ALGORITHMS: frozenset[str] = frozenset(
    {Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET, Algorithm.LEAKY_BUCKET}
)


class KeyScope(StrEnum):
    """What a limit is counted against."""

    USER = "user"
    API_KEY = "api_key"
    IP = "ip"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class LimitRule:
    """`limit` requests per `window_seconds`, enforced by `algorithm`.

    `burst` (bucket algorithms only) sets the bucket size separately from the
    average rate: 100 per minute on average, but up to 300 at once.
    """

    name: str
    limit: int
    window_seconds: float
    algorithm: str = Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET
    burst: int | None = None

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.name.strip():
            raise InvalidRuleError("rule name must not be blank")
        if self.limit < 1:
            raise InvalidRuleError(f"{self.name}: limit must be >= 1, got {self.limit}")
        if self.window_seconds <= 0:
            raise InvalidRuleError(
                f"{self.name}: window_seconds must be > 0, got {self.window_seconds}"
            )
        if self.burst is not None:
            if self.algorithm not in BUCKET_ALGORITHMS:
                raise InvalidRuleError(
                    f"{self.name}: burst only applies to bucket algorithms, "
                    f"not {self.algorithm}"
                )
            if self.burst < 1:
                raise InvalidRuleError(f"{self.name}: burst must be >= 1, got {self.burst}")

    @property
    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """The most requests that can pass at one instant."""
        return self.burst if self.burst is not None else self.limit

    @property
    def rate_per_second(self) -> float:
        """The long-run average rate the rule allows."""
        return self.limit / self.window_seconds


def _default_tiers() -> dict[str, LimitRule]:
    rules = (
        LimitRule("anonymous", 30, 60.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER),
        LimitRule("free", 100, 60.0, Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET),
        LimitRule("pro", 1_000, 60.0, Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET, burst=2_000),
        LimitRule("partner", 100_000, 86_400.0, Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW),
    )
    return {rule.name: rule for rule in rules}


def _default_scope_tiers() -> dict[KeyScope, str]:
    return {KeyScope.IP: "anonymous", KeyScope.USER: "free", KeyScope.API_KEY: "free"}


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RateLimiterConfig:
    """The tier table plus the limiter's operational knobs.

    tiers                  -- tier name -> rule; the key must equal rule.name
    default_tier_by_scope  -- tier used when a client key carries no tier
    idle_grace_seconds     -- extra time an idle key is kept past its reset point
    sweep_interval_seconds -- how often the background sweeper purges idle keys
    fail_open              -- on a store failure: allow (True) or refuse (False)
    """

    tiers: dict[str, LimitRule] = field(default_factory=_default_tiers)
    default_tier_by_scope: dict[KeyScope, str] = field(default_factory=_default_scope_tiers)
    idle_grace_seconds: float = 5.0
    sweep_interval_seconds: float = 30.0
    fail_open: bool = True

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.tiers:
            raise ConfigError("at least one tier is required")
        for tier_name, rule in self.tiers.items():
            if tier_name != rule.name:
                raise ConfigError(f"tier key {tier_name!r} does not match rule {rule.name!r}")
        for scope, tier_name in self.default_tier_by_scope.items():
            if tier_name not in self.tiers:
                raise ConfigError(f"scope {scope} defaults to unknown tier {tier_name!r}")
        if self.idle_grace_seconds < 0:
            raise ConfigError("idle_grace_seconds must be >= 0")
        if self.sweep_interval_seconds <= 0:
            raise ConfigError("sweep_interval_seconds must be > 0")

What to notice. LimitRule.algorithm is typed str, not Algorithm. The enum is a set of well-known names, and because StrEnum members are strings they fit the field directly. A custom algorithm can still register under any other name without editing this file. burst is rejected on window algorithms: a fixed window has no bucket for a burst to fill, and silently ignoring the field would be worse than refusing it.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "
from rate_limiter.config import RateLimiterConfig, LimitRule, Algorithm
from rate_limiter.errors import InvalidRuleError
pro = RateLimiterConfig().tiers['pro']
print(pro.capacity, round(pro.rate_per_second, 2))
try:
    LimitRule('bad', 10, 60.0, Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW, burst=20)
except InvalidRuleError as e:
    print('expected:', e)"

Output:

2000 16.67
expected: bad: burst only applies to bucket algorithms, not fixed_window

Step 3 — The clock

Goal: make time a seam. The limiter is nothing but arithmetic on time, so this seam matters more here than in any earlier chapter.

Type rate_limiter/clock.py:

"""The injectable clock. Rate limiting is arithmetic on time, so time is a seam.

Times are plain float seconds from a monotonic source. Wall-clock time can jump
backwards (NTP, daylight saving); a limiter fed by it would refill buckets twice.
"""
import threading
import time
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Clock(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def now(self) -> float:
        """Seconds since an arbitrary, fixed origin. Never decreases."""


class MonotonicClock(Clock):
    """Production clock: time.monotonic()."""

    def now(self) -> float:
        return time.monotonic()


class ManualClock(Clock):
    """Test clock that only moves when told to. Safe to share across threads."""

    def __init__(self, start: float = 0.0) -> None:
        self._now = start
        self._lock = threading.Lock()  # guards _now

    def now(self) -> float:
        with self._lock:
            return self._now

    def advance(self, seconds: float) -> None:
        if seconds < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"a monotonic clock cannot go back ({seconds})")
        with self._lock:
            self._now += seconds

What to notice. The clock returns float seconds, not a datetime. A rate limiter never needs the calendar; it needs differences. Floats make elapsed * rate one multiplication. ManualClock has a lock because the concurrency test shares it across forty threads.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "from rate_limiter.clock import ManualClock; c = ManualClock(1000.0); c.advance(2.5); print(c.now())"

Output:

1002.5

Step 4 — The decision, and its HTTP face

Goal: type the one object every algorithm returns, and its mapping to status code and headers.

Type rate_limiter/decision.py:

"""The answer to "may this request pass?", and how it maps onto HTTP.

Every algorithm returns the same Decision, so the HTTP layer never needs to
know which algorithm made it.
"""
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from http import HTTPStatus


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Decision:
    """One rate-limit verdict.

    allowed     -- may the request proceed?
    limit       -- the most requests that can pass at once under this rule
    remaining   -- how many more would pass right now
    retry_after -- seconds until this same request would pass (0 when allowed)
    reset_after -- seconds until the key is back to a full quota
    delay       -- leaky bucket only: wait this long before doing the work
    degraded    -- True when the store failed and the limiter failed open
    """

    allowed: bool
    limit: int
    remaining: int
    retry_after: float
    reset_after: float
    delay: float = 0.0
    degraded: bool = False

    @property
    def status_code(self) -> int:
        return int(HTTPStatus.OK if self.allowed else HTTPStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS)

    def headers(self) -> dict[str, str]:
        """RateLimit-* response headers, plus Retry-After on a 429.

        HTTP wants whole seconds, so times round UP: telling a client to come
        back in 0 seconds when the true answer is 0.3 guarantees another 429.
        A degraded decision sends no headers rather than invented numbers.
        """
        if self.degraded:
            return {}
        headers = {
            "RateLimit-Limit": str(self.limit),
            "RateLimit-Remaining": str(self.remaining),
            "RateLimit-Reset": str(_whole_seconds(self.reset_after)),
        }
        if not self.allowed:
            headers["Retry-After"] = str(max(1, _whole_seconds(self.retry_after)))
        return headers


def _whole_seconds(seconds: float) -> int:
    # Round to milliseconds first so float dust (2.0000000001) doesn't add a second.
    return math.ceil(round(seconds, 3))

What to notice. Rounding direction is a correctness issue here, not style. Retry-After: 0 for a true wait of 0.3 seconds invites an instant retry and a second 429. Rounding up, with a floor of 1, sends the client back when the request will actually pass. The RateLimit-* names follow the IETF httpapi rate-limit headers draft; many APIs still send the older X-RateLimit-* spellings, and adding them is a one-line change in this one method.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "
from rate_limiter.decision import Decision
d = Decision(allowed=False, limit=100, remaining=0, retry_after=2.4, reset_after=30.0)
print(d.status_code, d.headers())"

Output:

429 {'RateLimit-Limit': '100', 'RateLimit-Remaining': '0', 'RateLimit-Reset': '30', 'Retry-After': '3'}

Step 5 — Five algorithms, one interface

Goal: type the RateLimitAlgorithm contract and all five implementations. This is the longest file in the chapter and the one interviewers probe hardest. Type it slowly.

Type rate_limiter/algorithms.py:

"""Five rate-limiting algorithms behind one interface.

Each algorithm is a pure function of (old state, rule, now, cost) to
(new state, decision). No clock, no lock, no I/O. That purity is what lets the
same step run inside an in-memory lock today and inside a Redis Lua script later.
"""
import math
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass

from .config import Algorithm, LimitRule
from .decision import Decision


class RateLimitAlgorithm[S](ABC):
    """The contract every algorithm honours.

    apply()    -- decide one request and return the key's next state.
                  `state` is None for a key never seen (or already expired).
    idle_ttl() -- seconds after a key's last request at which its state is
                  indistinguishable from a fresh key. Past that, it can be deleted.
    """

    name: str

    @abstractmethod
    def apply(self, state: S | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float, cost: int) -> tuple[S, Decision]:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        ...


def _allow(rule: LimitRule, remaining: float, reset_after: float, delay: float = 0.0) -> Decision:
    return Decision(True, rule.capacity, max(0, math.floor(remaining)), 0.0, reset_after, delay)


def _deny(rule: LimitRule, remaining: float, retry_after: float, reset_after: float) -> Decision:
    return Decision(False, rule.capacity, max(0, math.floor(remaining)), retry_after, reset_after)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- buckets

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class BucketState:
    level: float        # tokens left (token bucket) or water held (leaky bucket)
    updated_at: float


class TokenBucket(RateLimitAlgorithm[BucketState]):
    """A bucket of `capacity` tokens refilling at `rate_per_second`.

    Allows bursts up to capacity, then the average rate. Two floats per key.
    """

    name = Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET

    def apply(self, state: BucketState | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float,
              cost: int) -> tuple[BucketState, Decision]:
        capacity, rate = rule.capacity, rule.rate_per_second
        if state is None:
            tokens = float(capacity)
        else:
            elapsed = max(0.0, now - state.updated_at)  # never refill on a clock step back
            tokens = min(float(capacity), state.level + elapsed * rate)
        if tokens >= cost:
            tokens -= cost
            decision = _allow(rule, tokens, (capacity - tokens) / rate)
        else:
            decision = _deny(rule, tokens, (cost - tokens) / rate, (capacity - tokens) / rate)
        return BucketState(tokens, now), decision

    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        return rule.capacity / rule.rate_per_second


class LeakyBucket(RateLimitAlgorithm[BucketState]):
    """A queue of `capacity` slots draining at `rate_per_second`.

    It shapes rather than polices: an admitted request gets a `delay`, the time
    its place in the queue takes to reach the front. Output is perfectly smooth.
    """

    name = Algorithm.LEAKY_BUCKET

    def apply(self, state: BucketState | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float,
              cost: int) -> tuple[BucketState, Decision]:
        capacity, rate = rule.capacity, rule.rate_per_second
        if state is None:
            level = 0.0
        else:
            elapsed = max(0.0, now - state.updated_at)
            level = max(0.0, state.level - elapsed * rate)
        if level + cost <= capacity:
            delay = level / rate
            level += cost
            decision = _allow(rule, capacity - level, level / rate, delay)
        else:
            decision = _deny(rule, capacity - level, (level + cost - capacity) / rate, level / rate)
        return BucketState(level, now), decision

    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        return rule.capacity / rule.rate_per_second


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- windows

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class WindowState:
    window: int         # index of the window: floor(now / window_seconds)
    count: int


class FixedWindow(RateLimitAlgorithm[WindowState]):
    """A counter per aligned window. Cheapest of all, but up to 2x the limit
    can pass across a window boundary."""

    name = Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW

    def apply(self, state: WindowState | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float,
              cost: int) -> tuple[WindowState, Decision]:
        size = rule.window_seconds
        window = math.floor(now / size)
        count = state.count if state is not None and state.window == window else 0
        until_next = (window + 1) * size - now
        if count + cost <= rule.limit:
            count += cost
            decision = _allow(rule, rule.limit - count, until_next)
        else:
            decision = _deny(rule, rule.limit - count, until_next, until_next)
        return WindowState(window, count), decision

    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        return rule.window_seconds


@dataclass(slots=True)
class LogState:
    stamps: deque[float]   # one timestamp per admitted unit of cost, oldest first


class SlidingWindowLog(RateLimitAlgorithm[LogState]):
    """Exact: remembers every admitted request in the last window.

    Memory is O(limit) per key, so it suits small limits only.
    The deque is mutated in place; the store calls apply() under its lock.
    """

    name = Algorithm.SLIDING_LOG

    def apply(self, state: LogState | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float,
              cost: int) -> tuple[LogState, Decision]:
        size = rule.window_seconds
        stamps = deque() if state is None else state.stamps
        while stamps and stamps[0] <= now - size:   # the window is (now - size, now]
            stamps.popleft()
        if len(stamps) + cost <= rule.limit:
            stamps.extend([now] * cost)
            decision = _allow(rule, rule.limit - len(stamps), stamps[-1] + size - now)
        else:
            # The request fits once enough of the oldest entries have aged out.
            must_expire = len(stamps) + cost - rule.limit
            retry_after = stamps[must_expire - 1] + size - now
            decision = _deny(rule, rule.limit - len(stamps), retry_after, stamps[-1] + size - now)
        return LogState(stamps), decision

    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        return rule.window_seconds


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CounterState:
    window: int
    current: int        # admitted in the current window
    previous: int       # admitted in the window before it


class SlidingWindowCounter(RateLimitAlgorithm[CounterState]):
    """Two counters and a weighted estimate of the sliding window.

    estimate = previous * (share of the previous window still inside the
    sliding window) + current. Near-exact, and O(1) memory per key.
    """

    name = Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER

    def apply(self, state: CounterState | None, rule: LimitRule, now: float,
              cost: int) -> tuple[CounterState, Decision]:
        size = rule.window_seconds
        window = math.floor(now / size)
        if state is None or state.window < window - 1:
            current, previous = 0, 0
        elif state.window == window - 1:
            current, previous = 0, state.current
        else:
            current, previous = state.current, state.previous
        elapsed = now - window * size
        estimate = previous * (size - elapsed) / size + current
        if estimate + cost <= rule.limit:
            current += cost
            decision = _allow(rule, rule.limit - estimate - cost,
                              self._reset_after(current, previous, elapsed, size))
        else:
            retry_after = self._retry_after(current, previous, elapsed, size, rule.limit, cost)
            decision = _deny(rule, rule.limit - estimate, retry_after,
                             self._reset_after(current, previous, elapsed, size))
        return CounterState(window, current, previous), decision

    @staticmethod
    def _retry_after(current: int, previous: int, elapsed: float, size: float,
                     limit: int, cost: int) -> float:
        room = limit - cost - current
        if room >= 0 and previous > 0:
            # Fits later in this window, once the previous window's weight decays:
            # previous * (size - t) / size <= room.
            return size * (1 - room / previous) - elapsed
        until_next = size - elapsed
        room_next = limit - cost
        if current <= room_next:
            return until_next
        # In the next window, this window's count decays the same way.
        return until_next + size * (1 - room_next / current)

    @staticmethod
    def _reset_after(current: int, previous: int, elapsed: float, size: float) -> float:
        if current > 0:
            return 2 * size - elapsed
        if previous > 0:
            return size - elapsed
        return 0.0

    def idle_ttl(self, rule: LimitRule) -> float:
        return 2 * rule.window_seconds


def default_algorithms() -> dict[str, RateLimitAlgorithm]:
    """The built-in registry, keyed by Algorithm name."""
    algorithms: tuple[RateLimitAlgorithm, ...] = (
        TokenBucket(), LeakyBucket(), FixedWindow(), SlidingWindowLog(), SlidingWindowCounter(),
    )
    return {algorithm.name: algorithm for algorithm in algorithms}

What to notice. Read the five apply methods as one family. Each one does the same three things: bring the state up to now (refill, drain, roll the window, drop old stamps), test whether cost fits, then build the next state and a Decision.

The interesting differences are in the retry_after arithmetic. Token bucket: the missing tokens divided by the refill rate. Fixed window: time to the next boundary. Sliding log: the moment the right old entry ages out. If one request needs three units and the log is full, three entries must leave, so the answer is the third-oldest stamp plus one window. The sliding counter is the subtle one. Either the previous window's weight decays enough within this window, or you wait for the next window, where today's count becomes tomorrow's decaying "previous". Both cases solve the same equation, previous × (size − t) / size + current + cost ≤ limit, for t.

The leaky bucket returns a delay on success. That is the real difference from the token bucket. Both keep "level and timestamp", but the token bucket polices (pass now or refuse), while the leaky bucket shapes (pass, but only after your turn in the queue).

Checkpoint — the purity, live. No limiter, no store, no clock; just state in, state out:

python3 -c "
from rate_limiter.algorithms import TokenBucket
from rate_limiter.config import LimitRule
rule = LimitRule('demo', 2, 10.0)
tb = TokenBucket()
state = None
for now in (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 5.0):
    state, d = tb.apply(state, rule, now, 1)
    print(now, d.allowed, d.remaining, round(d.retry_after, 2))"

Output:

0.0 True 1 0.0
0.0 True 0 0.0
0.0 False 0 5.0
5.0 True 0 0.0

Step 6 — The storage seam

Goal: type the StateStore contract and its in-memory implementation, with an expiry on every key.

Type rate_limiter/store.py:

"""The storage seam: where per-key state lives, and how it is updated atomically.

The whole contract is one method, update(): read a key's state, run the
algorithm's step on it, write the result back with an expiry, all as one atomic
unit. In memory that is a lock. In Redis it is a Lua script (see the chapter's
follow-ups); the limiter cannot tell the difference.
"""
import logging
import threading
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class StateStore(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def update[R](self, key: str, now: float, ttl: float,
                  step: Callable[[Any | None], tuple[Any, R]]) -> R:
        """Atomically apply `step` to the key's state and return its result.

        `step` receives None when the key is missing or expired. Its new state is
        stored with an expiry of now + ttl. Raises StoreError if the store fails.
        """

    @abstractmethod
    def purge_expired(self, now: float) -> int:
        """Delete every key whose expiry has passed. Returns how many went."""

    @abstractmethod
    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """Number of keys currently held, expired or not."""


@dataclass(slots=True)
class _Entry:
    state: Any
    expires_at: float


class InMemoryStore(StateStore):
    """A dict of key -> (state, expiry), guarded by one lock.

    One lock is the simplest correct choice: every update is O(1) or O(limit)
    and short. Lock striping is the next step if profiling ever says so.
    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._entries: dict[str, _Entry] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()  # guards _entries and every state object in it

    def update[R](self, key: str, now: float, ttl: float,
                  step: Callable[[Any | None], tuple[Any, R]]) -> R:
        with self._lock:
            entry = self._entries.get(key)
            state = entry.state if entry is not None and entry.expires_at > now else None
            new_state, result = step(state)
            self._entries[key] = _Entry(new_state, now + ttl)
            return result

    def purge_expired(self, now: float) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            expired = [key for key, entry in self._entries.items() if entry.expires_at <= now]
            for key in expired:
                del self._entries[key]
        if expired:
            log.info("purged %d idle rate-limit keys", len(expired))
        return len(expired)

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return len(self._entries)

What to notice. An expired entry reads as None, exactly as if it had already been purged. So correctness never depends on when the sweeper last ran. The sweep only frees memory. Redis behaves the same way: a key past its PEXPIRE is gone on read, whether or not the background expiry cycle has reached it yet. Also note that purge_expired logs after releasing the lock. Never do slow work, and logging can be slow, while every request thread waits on you.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "

s = InMemoryStore()
bump = lambda count: ((count or 0) + 1, (count or 0) + 1)
print(s.update('k', 0.0, 10.0, bump), s.update('k', 5.0, 10.0, bump))
print('after expiry:', s.update('k', 20.0, 10.0, bump))
print('purged:', s.purge_expired(40.0), 'left:', len(s))"

Output:

1 2
after expiry: 1

Step 7 — Keys and the rule book

Goal: type ClientKey (who is asking) and RuleBook (which rule applies to them).

Type rate_limiter/rules.py:

"""Who is asking, and which rule applies to them.

ClientKey names the thing being limited (a user, an API key, an IP).
RuleBook turns a ClientKey into a LimitRule using the tier table.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass

from .config import KeyScope, LimitRule, RateLimiterConfig
from .errors import InvalidKeyError, UnknownTierError


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class ClientKey:
    """One limited identity. `tier` overrides the scope's default tier."""

    scope: KeyScope
    value: str
    tier: str | None = None

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.value.strip():
            raise InvalidKeyError(f"{self.scope} key must not be blank")

    def storage_key(self, rule: LimitRule) -> str:
        """The store key. Rule and algorithm are part of it, so a plan change
        starts a fresh counter and two algorithms never read each other's state."""
        return f"rl:{rule.name}:{rule.algorithm}:{self.scope}:{self.value}"


class RuleBook:
    """Resolves the rule for a client: explicit tier first, then the scope default."""

    def __init__(self, config: RateLimiterConfig) -> None:
        self._config = config

    def rule_for(self, client: ClientKey) -> LimitRule:
        tier = client.tier or self._config.default_tier_by_scope.get(client.scope)
        if tier is None:
            raise UnknownTierError(f"no tier given and no default for scope {client.scope}")
        rule = self._config.tiers.get(tier)
        if rule is None:
            raise UnknownTierError(f"unknown tier {tier!r}")
        return rule

    def rules(self) -> list[LimitRule]:
        return list(self._config.tiers.values())

What to notice. RuleBook is small today: two dictionary lookups. It is still its own class, because rule resolution is where the requirements grow. Per-endpoint rules, a per-customer override pulled from a database, a temporary ban list: all of them land in rule_for, and the limiter never changes.

Checkpoint:

python3 -c "
from rate_limiter.rules import ClientKey, RuleBook
from rate_limiter.config import RateLimiterConfig, KeyScope
book = RuleBook(RateLimiterConfig())
ip = ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, '203.0.113.7')
rule = book.rule_for(ip)
print(rule.name, rule.limit, rule.algorithm)
print(ip.storage_key(rule))
print(book.rule_for(ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, 'u1', tier='pro')).capacity)"

Output:

anonymous 30 sliding_counter
rl:anonymous:sliding_counter:ip:203.0.113.7
2000

Step 8 — The limiter and the sweeper

Goal: type RateLimiter, the class that ties rule, algorithm, store and clock together. Then type IdleKeySweeper, which keeps memory bounded.

Type rate_limiter/limiter.py:

"""The rate limiter: resolve the rule, run the algorithm in the store, decide.

It holds no mutable state of its own. All per-key state lives in the store,
which is what makes the same class work in one process or across a fleet.
"""
import logging
import threading
from collections.abc import Mapping

from .algorithms import RateLimitAlgorithm, default_algorithms
from .clock import Clock, MonotonicClock
from .config import LimitRule, RateLimiterConfig
from .decision import Decision
from .errors import (
    ConfigError,
    InvalidCostError,
    LimiterUnavailableError,
    StoreError,
    UnknownAlgorithmError,
)
from .rules import ClientKey, RuleBook
from .store import InMemoryStore, StateStore

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: RateLimiterConfig | None = None,
        *,
        store: StateStore | None = None,
        clock: Clock | None = None,
        algorithms: Mapping[str, RateLimitAlgorithm] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        # `is None`, not `or`: an empty store defines __len__ == 0, so it is falsy.
        self._config = config if config is not None else RateLimiterConfig()
        self._store = store if store is not None else InMemoryStore()
        self._clock = clock if clock is not None else MonotonicClock()
        self._algorithms = dict(algorithms) if algorithms is not None else default_algorithms()
        self._rules = RuleBook(self._config)
        for rule in self._rules.rules():  # fail at startup, not on the first request
            if rule.algorithm not in self._algorithms:
                raise UnknownAlgorithmError(f"{rule.name}: no algorithm named {rule.algorithm!r}")

    def check(self, client: ClientKey, cost: int = 1) -> Decision:
        """Decide one request of `cost` units for `client`, and record it if allowed."""
        rule = self._rules.rule_for(client)
        if not 1 <= cost <= rule.capacity:
            raise InvalidCostError(f"cost must be between 1 and {rule.capacity}, got {cost}")
        algorithm = self._algorithms[rule.algorithm]
        now = self._clock.now()
        ttl = algorithm.idle_ttl(rule) + self._config.idle_grace_seconds
        try:
            decision = self._store.update(
                client.storage_key(rule), now, ttl,
                lambda state: algorithm.apply(state, rule, now, cost),
            )
        except StoreError as exc:
            return self._on_store_failure(rule, exc)
        if not decision.allowed:
            # DEBUG, not INFO: a client hammering a 429 would flood the logs.
            log.debug("denied %s:%s on %s, retry in %.3fs",
                      client.scope, client.value, rule.name, decision.retry_after)
        return decision

    @property
    def config(self) -> RateLimiterConfig:
        return self._config

    def sweep_idle(self) -> int:
        """Purge keys idle past their reset point. Returns how many were removed."""
        return self._store.purge_expired(self._clock.now())

    def _on_store_failure(self, rule: LimitRule, exc: StoreError) -> Decision:
        if self._config.fail_open:
            log.warning("rate-limit store failed, failing open for %s: %s", rule.name, exc)
            return Decision(True, rule.capacity, rule.capacity, 0.0, 0.0, degraded=True)
        log.error("rate-limit store failed, failing closed for %s: %s", rule.name, exc)
        raise LimiterUnavailableError(f"rate-limit store unavailable: {exc}") from exc


class IdleKeySweeper:
    """Background thread that calls limiter.sweep_idle() every interval.

    Use as a context manager, or call start() and stop() yourself.
    """

    def __init__(self, limiter: RateLimiter, interval_seconds: float | None = None) -> None:
        interval = limiter.config.sweep_interval_seconds if interval_seconds is None else interval_seconds
        if interval <= 0:
            raise ConfigError(f"sweep interval must be > 0, got {interval}")
        self._limiter = limiter
        self._interval = interval
        self._stop = threading.Event()
        self._thread: threading.Thread | None = None

    def start(self) -> None:
        if self._thread is not None:
            raise RuntimeError("sweeper already started")
        self._thread = threading.Thread(target=self._run, name="rate-limit-sweeper", daemon=True)
        self._thread.start()

    def stop(self) -> None:
        self._stop.set()
        if self._thread is not None:
            self._thread.join()

    def _run(self) -> None:
        while not self._stop.wait(self._interval):
            try:
                self._limiter.sweep_idle()
            except StoreError:
                log.exception("idle-key sweep failed; will retry next interval")

    def __enter__(self) -> "IdleKeySweeper":
        self.start()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc_info: object) -> None:
        self.stop()

What to notice. Look at the comment above the constructor's defaults. The first draft of this file said store or InMemoryStore(), and a test caught it. StateStore defines __len__, so an empty store is falsy, and or quietly threw away the store the caller passed in. Use x if x is not None else default for any injected object that might define __len__ or __bool__.

Two more things. The constructor checks every rule's algorithm against the registry, so a typo in config fails at startup, not on the first request at 3 a.m. And now is read once per call, outside the store, then captured by the lambda. The algorithm, the expiry and the decision all agree on the same instant.

Step 10 — A runnable slice

Goal: watch the whole story with a manual clock: tiers and 429 headers, the boundary burst under all five algorithms, leaky-bucket shaping, and idle cleanup.

Type rate_limiter/__main__.py:

"""Demo: python3 -m rate_limiter

A manual clock makes every number below reproducible.
"""
from . import (
    Algorithm,
    ClientKey,
    KeyScope,
    LimitRule,
    ManualClock,
    RateLimiter,
    RateLimiterConfig,
)

START = 1_000.0


def per_key_limits() -> None:
    print("== per-key limits and tiers ==")
    clock = ManualClock(START)
    limiter = RateLimiter(RateLimiterConfig(
        tiers={
            "anonymous": LimitRule("anonymous", 2, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER),
            "free": LimitRule("free", 3, 10.0, Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET),
            "pro": LimitRule("pro", 10, 10.0, Algorithm.TOKEN_BUCKET),
        },
        default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.IP: "anonymous", KeyScope.USER: "free"},
    ), clock=clock)
    alice = ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "alice")
    for attempt in range(1, 5):
        d = limiter.check(alice)
        print(f"alice #{attempt}: {d.status_code} remaining={d.remaining}")
    print("alice 429 headers:", limiter.check(alice).headers())
    bob = ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "bob", tier="pro")
    d = limiter.check(bob)
    print(f"bob (pro) right after: {d.status_code} remaining={d.remaining}")
    ip = ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "203.0.113.7")
    print("anonymous IP:", [limiter.check(ip).status_code for _ in range(3)])
    clock.advance(4.0)
    print("alice after 4s:", limiter.check(alice).status_code)


def boundary_burst() -> None:
    print("== 5 requests at t=9.9s, 5 more at t=10.1s, limit 5 per 10s ==")
    for algorithm in Algorithm:
        clock = ManualClock(START - 0.1)  # 0.1s before a window boundary
        limiter = RateLimiter(RateLimiterConfig(
            tiers={"t": LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, algorithm)},
            default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.USER: "t"},
        ), clock=clock)
        user = ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "u")
        allowed = sum(limiter.check(user).allowed for _ in range(5))
        clock.advance(0.2)
        allowed += sum(limiter.check(user).allowed for _ in range(5))
        print(f"{algorithm:<16} allowed {allowed:>2} of 10 within 0.2s")


def leaky_shaping() -> None:
    print("== leaky bucket shapes: 4 requests at once, 1 per second drain ==")
    limiter = RateLimiter(RateLimiterConfig(
        tiers={"q": LimitRule("q", 1, 1.0, Algorithm.LEAKY_BUCKET, burst=3)},
        default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.API_KEY: "q"},
    ), clock=ManualClock(START))
    key = ClientKey(KeyScope.API_KEY, "k-123")
    for _ in range(4):
        d = limiter.check(key)
        print(f"allowed={d.allowed} delay={d.delay:.1f}s retry_after={d.retry_after:.1f}s")


def idle_cleanup() -> None:
    print("== idle-key cleanup ==")
    clock = ManualClock(START)
    limiter = RateLimiter(RateLimiterConfig(
        tiers={"free": LimitRule("free", 5, 60.0)},
        default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.IP: "free"},
        idle_grace_seconds=5.0,
    ), clock=clock)
    for n in range(1000):
        limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, f"10.0.{n // 256}.{n % 256}"))
    clock.advance(30.0)
    limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "10.0.0.0"))  # one key stays active
    clock.advance(40.0)
    print("purged after 70s:", limiter.sweep_idle())
    clock.advance(30.0)
    print("purged after 100s:", limiter.sweep_idle())


def main() -> None:
    per_key_limits()
    boundary_burst()
    leaky_shaping()
    idle_cleanup()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What to notice. The boundary-burst section is the whole algorithm debate in five lines of output. Read the fixed-window row and remember it. Five requests just before the boundary and five just after all pass: twice the limit in 0.2 seconds. Every other algorithm holds the line at 5. The cleanup section shows the TTL at work: 999 keys idle for 70 seconds are purged, while the one key touched at 30 seconds survives until its own expiry.

Step 11 — The test suite

Goal: type the full suite. Most of it is one contract applied to all five algorithms.

Type tests/__init__.py (empty), then tests/test_rate_limiter.py:

"""Tests for the rate limiter. Time is a ManualClock throughout; nothing sleeps
except the one test that exercises the real background sweeper thread."""
import threading
import time
import unittest

from rate_limiter import (
    Algorithm,
    ClientKey,
    ConfigError,
    Decision,
    IdleKeySweeper,
    InMemoryStore,
    InvalidCostError,
    InvalidKeyError,
    InvalidRuleError,
    KeyScope,
    LimitRule,
    LimiterUnavailableError,
    ManualClock,
    RateLimitAlgorithm,
    RateLimiter,
    RateLimiterConfig,
    StoreError,
    TokenBucket,
    UnknownAlgorithmError,
    UnknownTierError,
)

START = 1_000.0          # a window boundary for every window size used below
LIMIT, WINDOW = 5, 10.0  # the contract tests' rule: 5 requests per 10 seconds
TINY = 1e-6
USER = ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "alice")


def make_limiter(rule, clock=None, store=None, **config_kwargs):
    clock = clock or ManualClock(START)
    config = RateLimiterConfig(
        tiers={rule.name: rule},
        default_tier_by_scope={scope: rule.name for scope in KeyScope},
        **config_kwargs,
    )
    return RateLimiter(config, clock=clock, store=store), clock


def drain(limiter, client=USER, n=LIMIT):
    return [limiter.check(client) for _ in range(n)]


class AlgorithmContractTests(unittest.TestCase):
    """Liskov in practice: every algorithm must pass the same behavioural contract."""

    def each_algorithm(self):
        for algorithm in Algorithm:
            with self.subTest(algorithm=algorithm):
                yield make_limiter(LimitRule("t", LIMIT, WINDOW, algorithm))

    def test_fresh_key_allows_exactly_the_limit_then_denies(self):
        for limiter, _ in self.each_algorithm():
            self.assertTrue(all(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter)))
            denied = limiter.check(USER)
            self.assertFalse(denied.allowed)
            self.assertEqual(denied.status_code, 429)

    def test_retry_after_is_exact(self):
        for limiter, clock in self.each_algorithm():
            drain(limiter)
            retry_after = limiter.check(USER).retry_after
            self.assertGreater(retry_after, 0)
            clock.advance(retry_after - 0.01)
            self.assertFalse(limiter.check(USER).allowed, "too early must still be denied")
            clock.advance(0.01 + TINY)
            self.assertTrue(limiter.check(USER).allowed, "at retry_after it must pass")

    def test_full_quota_returns_after_idle_ttl(self):
        for limiter, clock in self.each_algorithm():
            drain(limiter)
            clock.advance(2 * WINDOW)
            self.assertTrue(all(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter)))

    def test_keys_are_independent(self):
        for limiter, _ in self.each_algorithm():
            drain(limiter)
            self.assertTrue(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "bob")).allowed)

    def test_decision_invariants(self):
        for limiter, _ in self.each_algorithm():
            for d in drain(limiter, n=LIMIT + 2):
                self.assertTrue(0 <= d.remaining <= d.limit)
                self.assertGreaterEqual(d.reset_after, 0)
                self.assertEqual(d.retry_after == 0, d.allowed)


class TokenBucketTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_refills_at_the_average_rate(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0))  # 0.5 tokens/s
        drain(limiter)
        clock.advance(4.0)  # two tokens back
        self.assertEqual([d.allowed for d in drain(limiter, n=3)], [True, True, False])

    def test_burst_is_separate_from_rate(self):
        limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, burst=8))
        results = drain(limiter, n=9)
        self.assertEqual(sum(d.allowed for d in results), 8)
        self.assertEqual(results[0].limit, 8)

    def test_cost_consumes_several_tokens(self):
        limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0))
        self.assertEqual(limiter.check(USER, cost=4).remaining, 1)
        denied = limiter.check(USER, cost=3)
        self.assertFalse(denied.allowed)
        self.assertEqual(denied.remaining, 1)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(denied.retry_after, 4.0)  # 2 missing tokens at 0.5/s

    def test_clock_step_back_never_adds_tokens(self):
        algorithm = TokenBucket()
        rule = LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0)
        state, _ = algorithm.apply(None, rule, 100.0, 5)
        _, decision = algorithm.apply(state, rule, 90.0, 1)
        self.assertFalse(decision.allowed)


class LeakyBucketTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_admitted_requests_are_queued_with_growing_delay(self):
        limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 1, 1.0, Algorithm.LEAKY_BUCKET, burst=3))
        results = drain(limiter, n=4)
        self.assertEqual([d.delay for d in results[:3]], [0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
        self.assertFalse(results[3].allowed)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(results[3].retry_after, 1.0)

    def test_queue_drains_over_time(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 1, 1.0, Algorithm.LEAKY_BUCKET, burst=3))
        drain(limiter, n=3)
        clock.advance(2.0)
        decision = limiter.check(USER)
        self.assertTrue(decision.allowed)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(decision.delay, 1.0)


class FixedWindowTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_counter_resets_at_the_boundary(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW))
        clock.advance(3.0)
        drain(limiter)
        denied = limiter.check(USER)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(denied.retry_after, 7.0)
        clock.advance(7.0)
        self.assertTrue(limiter.check(USER).allowed)

    def test_boundary_burst_lets_twice_the_limit_through(self):
        """The known weakness, pinned so nobody 'discovers' it in production."""
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(
            LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW), clock=ManualClock(START - 0.1))
        allowed = sum(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter))
        clock.advance(0.2)
        allowed += sum(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter))
        self.assertEqual(allowed, 10)


class SlidingWindowLogTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_boundary_burst_is_blocked(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(
            LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_LOG), clock=ManualClock(START - 0.1))
        drain(limiter)
        clock.advance(0.2)
        self.assertFalse(any(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter)))

    def test_each_entry_expires_exactly_one_window_later(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 2, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_LOG))
        limiter.check(USER)
        clock.advance(4.0)
        limiter.check(USER)
        denied = limiter.check(USER)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(denied.retry_after, 6.0)  # the t=0 entry leaves at t=10
        clock.advance(6.0)  # an entry exactly one window old is out
        self.assertTrue(limiter.check(USER).allowed)
        self.assertFalse(limiter.check(USER).allowed)


class SlidingWindowCounterTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_previous_window_is_weighted_by_overlap(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 10, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER))
        drain(limiter, n=10)
        clock.advance(17.0)  # previous=10, 30% of it still overlaps: estimate 3
        results = drain(limiter, n=8)
        self.assertEqual(sum(d.allowed for d in results), 7)

    def test_boundary_burst_is_blocked(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(
            LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER), clock=ManualClock(START - 0.1))
        drain(limiter)
        clock.advance(0.2)
        self.assertFalse(any(d.allowed for d in drain(limiter)))

    def test_two_idle_windows_forget_everything(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0, Algorithm.SLIDING_COUNTER))
        drain(limiter)
        clock.advance(20.0)
        self.assertEqual(limiter.check(USER).remaining, 4)


class DecisionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_allowed_headers(self):
        d = Decision(True, 100, 42, 0.0, 12.2)
        self.assertEqual(d.status_code, 200)
        self.assertEqual(d.headers(), {"RateLimit-Limit": "100", "RateLimit-Remaining": "42",
                                       "RateLimit-Reset": "13"})

    def test_denied_headers_round_up_and_never_say_zero(self):
        d = Decision(False, 100, 0, 0.2, 30.0)
        self.assertEqual(d.status_code, 429)
        self.assertEqual(d.headers()["Retry-After"], "1")
        self.assertEqual(Decision(False, 1, 0, 2.0000000001, 2.0).headers()["Retry-After"], "2")

    def test_degraded_decision_sends_no_headers(self):
        self.assertEqual(Decision(True, 5, 5, 0.0, 0.0, degraded=True).headers(), {})


class ConfigAndRuleTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_invalid_rules_are_rejected(self):
        for kwargs in ({"limit": 0, "window_seconds": 1.0},
                       {"limit": 1, "window_seconds": 0.0},
                       {"limit": 1, "window_seconds": 1.0, "algorithm": Algorithm.FIXED_WINDOW,
                        "burst": 5},
                       {"limit": 1, "window_seconds": 1.0, "burst": 0}):
            with self.subTest(kwargs=kwargs), self.assertRaises(InvalidRuleError):
                LimitRule("bad", **kwargs)

    def test_config_rejects_dangling_tiers(self):
        rule = LimitRule("free", 5, 10.0)
        with self.assertRaises(ConfigError):
            RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"free": rule}, default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.IP: "gold"})
        with self.assertRaises(ConfigError):
            RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"paid": rule})

    def test_default_tiers_by_scope(self):
        limiter = RateLimiter(clock=ManualClock(START))
        self.assertEqual(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "198.51.100.4")).limit, 30)
        self.assertEqual(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.API_KEY, "k1")).limit, 100)
        self.assertEqual(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "u1", tier="pro")).limit, 2_000)

    def test_unknown_tier_and_blank_key_are_rejected(self):
        limiter = RateLimiter(clock=ManualClock(START))
        with self.assertRaises(UnknownTierError):
            limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "u1", tier="platinum"))
        with self.assertRaises(InvalidKeyError):
            ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "   ")

    def test_same_value_in_different_scopes_is_counted_separately(self):
        limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 1, 10.0))
        self.assertTrue(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.USER, "x")).allowed)
        self.assertTrue(limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.API_KEY, "x")).allowed)

    def test_cost_outside_bounds_is_rejected(self):
        limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0))
        for cost in (0, 6):
            with self.subTest(cost=cost), self.assertRaises(InvalidCostError):
                limiter.check(USER, cost=cost)


class AlwaysAllow(RateLimitAlgorithm[None]):
    name = "always_allow"

    def apply(self, state, rule, now, cost):
        return None, Decision(True, rule.capacity, rule.capacity, 0.0, 0.0)

    def idle_ttl(self, rule):
        return 0.0


class ExtensionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_custom_algorithm_plugs_in_without_edits(self):
        rule = LimitRule("internal", 1, 1.0, algorithm="always_allow")
        config = RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"internal": rule},
                                   default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.USER: "internal"})
        limiter = RateLimiter(config, algorithms={"always_allow": AlwaysAllow()})
        self.assertTrue(all(limiter.check(USER).allowed for _ in range(10)))

    def test_unregistered_algorithm_fails_at_startup(self):
        rule = LimitRule("internal", 1, 1.0, algorithm="gcra")
        config = RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"internal": rule}, default_tier_by_scope={})
        with self.assertRaises(UnknownAlgorithmError):
            RateLimiter(config)


class FailingStore(InMemoryStore):
    def update(self, key, now, ttl, step):
        raise StoreError("connection refused")


class StoreAndCleanupTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_sweep_removes_only_idle_keys(self):
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 60.0), idle_grace_seconds=5.0)
        limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "a"))
        clock.advance(30.0)
        limiter.check(ClientKey(KeyScope.IP, "b"))
        clock.advance(40.0)  # a idle 70s > 65s ttl; b idle 40s
        self.assertEqual(limiter.sweep_idle(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(limiter.sweep_idle(), 0)

    def test_expired_entry_reads_as_a_fresh_key(self):
        store = InMemoryStore()
        store.update("k", 0.0, 10.0, lambda state: ("old", None))
        seen = store.update("k", 10.0, 10.0, lambda state: (state, state))
        self.assertIsNone(seen)

    def test_background_sweeper_purges(self):
        store = InMemoryStore()
        limiter, clock = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0), store=store,
                                      idle_grace_seconds=0.0)
        limiter.check(USER)
        clock.advance(11.0)
        with IdleKeySweeper(limiter, interval_seconds=0.01):
            deadline = time.monotonic() + 2.0
            while len(store) and time.monotonic() < deadline:
                time.sleep(0.01)
        self.assertEqual(len(store), 0)

    def test_fail_open_allows_with_no_headers(self):
        config = RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"t": LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0)},
                                   default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.USER: "t"})
        limiter = RateLimiter(config, store=FailingStore())
        with self.assertLogs("rate_limiter.limiter", "WARNING"):
            decision = limiter.check(USER)
        self.assertTrue(decision.allowed and decision.degraded)
        self.assertEqual(decision.headers(), {})

    def test_fail_closed_raises(self):
        config = RateLimiterConfig(tiers={"t": LimitRule("t", 5, 10.0)},
                                   default_tier_by_scope={KeyScope.USER: "t"}, fail_open=False)
        limiter = RateLimiter(config, store=FailingStore())
        with self.assertLogs("rate_limiter.limiter", "ERROR"), \
                self.assertRaises(LimiterUnavailableError):
            limiter.check(USER)


class ConcurrencyTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_exactly_the_limit_passes_under_contention(self):
        threads_count, limit = 40, 10
        for algorithm in Algorithm:
            with self.subTest(algorithm=algorithm):
                limiter, _ = make_limiter(LimitRule("t", limit, 60.0, algorithm))
                barrier = threading.Barrier(threads_count)
                results: list[bool] = []
                results_lock = threading.Lock()

                def hit():
                    barrier.wait()
                    allowed = limiter.check(USER).allowed
                    with results_lock:
                        results.append(allowed)

                workers = [threading.Thread(target=hit) for _ in range(threads_count)]
                for worker in workers:
                    worker.start()
                for worker in workers:
                    worker.join()
                self.assertEqual(sum(results), limit)
                self.assertEqual(len(results), threads_count)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

What to notice. AlgorithmContractTests is Liskov written as code. Every algorithm, in a subTest, must allow exactly the limit, deny the next request, and pass at exactly retry_after but not 10 ms before. That last test is the sharpest one in the file: it checks the retry_after arithmetic of all five algorithms against their own apply. The concurrency test does the same across algorithms: forty threads behind a Barrier, exactly ten winners.

python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

8. Enterprise checklist, mapped to the code

# Practice Where it shows up here Why it matters
1 Single Responsibility Algorithms decide; StateStore stores atomically; RuleBook resolves tiers; Decision speaks HTTP Changing a header name touches one method; changing storage touches one class
2 Open/Closed New algorithm = new RateLimitAlgorithm + registry entry (AlwaysAllow in the tests); new store = new StateStore GCRA or Redis arrive without edits to the limiter
3 Liskov AlgorithmContractTests runs one contract over all five algorithms Any algorithm can back any tier

6 logging, not print Denials at DEBUG, store failure at WARNING/ERROR, purges at INFO; print only in __main__.py A 429 storm doesn't become a log storm
